input.question: If HIV is a retro virus, why can't we find a way to stop reverse transcriptase from working?
input.ground_truth: We do! [Reverse-transcriptase inhibitors](_URL_0_) are a class of anti-retroviral drugs that operate as you suggest. But we tend to see the same problem in highly targeted drugs acting on a disease that mutates easily (like HIV or cancer). The disease gains resistance to the drug by acquiring slight changes in the shape of the target protein.

Okay, let’s imagine HIV is like a little sneaky robot that wants to make copies of itself inside your body. This robot uses a special tool called "reverse transcriptase" to help it make new robot friends.

Now, scientists really want to stop this sneaky robot from making more copies, so they try to break the special tool, reverse transcriptase. They make medicines that can block or stop this tool from working.

But here’s why it’s hard:  
The robot’s tool can sometimes change a little bit, like if you change the shape of a toy so it doesn’t fit in the toy box anymore. When reverse transcriptase changes a little, the medicine can’t find it and stop it as easily. So, the robot keeps making new copies.

That’s why it’s tricky to stop reverse transcriptase all the time—it keeps changing and hiding! But scientists keep trying to make better medicines to catch the sneaky robot.
